title: Inheritance: genetic terminology and genetic crosses

curriculum.source_reference: Cambridge International AS & A Level Biology 9700 syllabus 2028-2030, Topic 16, pp. 42–44.

learning_objectives: Use the syllabus genetic terminology accurately.
Construct and interpret monohybrid and dihybrid genetic diagrams.
Predict outcomes involving dominance, codominance, multiple alleles and sex linkage.
Interpret autosomal linkage and epistasis crosses without memorising epistasis ratios.
Use test crosses to determine unknown genotypes.
sections: The genetic vocabulary

A gene is a length of DNA that influences a characteristic, often by coding for a polypeptide or functional RNA. A locus is the position of a gene on a chromosome. An allele is an alternative form of a gene. Genotype is the allele combination; phenotype is the observable characteristic resulting from genotype and environment.
Dominance and genotype terms

A dominant allele affects the phenotype in a heterozygote; a recessive allele is expressed in the phenotype only when no dominant allele masks it. Homozygous individuals have two identical alleles at a locus; heterozygous individuals have two different alleles. F1 is the first filial generation and F2 is the offspring generation from the F1.
Monohybrid crosses

A monohybrid cross follows one gene. For Aa × Aa, the gametes are A and a from each parent. The offspring genotypes are AA, Aa, Aa and aa, giving a 1:2:1 genotype ratio. With complete dominance, the phenotype ratio is 3 dominant : 1 recessive.
Codominance

In codominance, both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote. Neither allele masks the other. For example, if Iᴬ and Iᴮ alleles both produce their corresponding red-cell antigens, genotype IᴬIᴮ gives blood group AB. The heterozygote phenotype is distinct from both homozygotes.
Multiple alleles

A gene may have more than two alleles in a population, although a diploid individual carries only two alleles at that locus. The ABO blood group gene has Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i alleles. Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant to each other, and both are dominant to i.
Dihybrid crosses

A dihybrid cross follows two genes. If genes assort independently, an AaBb individual can form AB, Ab, aB and ab gametes in equal proportions. AaBb × AaBb gives the familiar 9:3:3:1 phenotype ratio only when both genes show complete dominance and assort independently.
Sex linkage

A sex-linked gene is located on a sex chromosome. For an X-linked recessive allele, males (XY) express the allele if it is present on their single X chromosome. Females (XX) usually need two copies to express the recessive phenotype; heterozygous females are carriers. Fathers pass their X chromosome to daughters and their Y chromosome to sons.
Autosomal linkage

Linked genes are on the same chromosome and tend to be inherited together. A heterozygote with linked alleles may produce more parental-type gametes than recombinant gametes. Crossing over between loci can produce recombinant gametes. The closer two loci are, the less likely a crossover occurs between them.
Epistasis

Epistasis occurs when an allele of one gene affects or masks the expression of another gene at a different locus. The phenotype depends on interaction between gene products. Work out the genotype-to-phenotype relationship from the information in the question; the syllabus does not require memorising expected ratios for different types of epistasis.
Test crosses

A test cross is a cross between an individual with a dominant phenotype but unknown genotype and a homozygous recessive individual. If the unknown is homozygous dominant, all offspring show the dominant phenotype. If heterozygous, a 1:1 dominant:recessive ratio is expected for a monohybrid cross.
Constructing a genetic diagram

State parental phenotypes and genotypes, list gametes, show the cross, then give offspring genotypes and phenotypes with a ratio or probability. Define allele symbols clearly. For sex linkage, write alleles as superscripts on X chromosomes and show the sex chromosomes in each offspring.
Probability and independent events

For independent events, multiply probabilities to find the probability that both occur. Add probabilities for mutually exclusive routes to the same outcome. A predicted ratio is an expectation for many offspring; a small family may deviate by chance.

questions.question: Define gene, locus and allele.
questions.answer: A gene is a DNA sequence influencing a characteristic; a locus is its position on a chromosome; an allele is an alternative form of a gene.

questions.question: Distinguish genotype from phenotype.
questions.answer: Genotype is the allele combination an organism has; phenotype is its observable characteristics resulting from genotype and environmental effects.

questions.question: For Aa × Aa, state the genotype ratio and phenotype ratio assuming complete dominance.
questions.answer: Genotype ratio 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa; phenotype ratio 3 dominant : 1 recessive.

questions.question: Explain codominance using ABO blood groups.
questions.answer: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are both expressed in an IᴬIᴮ heterozygote, producing both A and B antigens and blood group AB.

questions.question: Why are there three ABO alleles in the population but only two in one diploid individual?
questions.answer: The population has three alternative alleles, but a diploid individual has only two homologous chromosomes and therefore carries at most two alleles at the locus.

questions.question: Give the gametes produced by AaBb if the genes assort independently.
questions.answer: AB, Ab, aB and ab, in equal proportions if there is no linkage and no segregation distortion.

questions.question: Under what conditions is a 9:3:3:1 dihybrid phenotype ratio expected?
questions.answer: When two genes assort independently, both show complete dominance, and the heterozygous F1 individuals produce the four gamete types in equal proportions.

questions.question: A woman is a carrier of an X-linked recessive allele and the man is unaffected. What proportion of their sons are expected to be affected?
questions.answer: One half of their sons are expected to inherit the affected X chromosome from their mother and express the recessive allele.

questions.question: Why can an affected father not pass an X-linked allele directly to his son?
questions.answer: A father passes his Y chromosome, not his X chromosome, to a son.

questions.question: What is autosomal linkage?
questions.answer: Two or more genes located on the same autosome tend to be inherited together, although crossing over can produce recombinant combinations.

questions.question: A test cross produces 1:1 dominant and recessive offspring. What is the likely genotype of the tested parent?
questions.answer: Heterozygous, because crossing it with a homozygous recessive individual gives half heterozygous dominant-phenotype offspring and half homozygous recessive offspring.

questions.question: Define epistasis.
questions.answer: An allele of one gene affects or masks the expression of another gene at a different locus.

questions.question: A heterozygous tall plant is test crossed with a dwarf plant. Give the expected offspring ratio.
questions.answer: Tt × tt produces 1 Tt tall : 1 tt dwarf, so 1:1.

questions.question: A couple have a 1/2 probability of a child being male and a 1/4 probability of inheriting a specified autosomal genotype. Assuming independence, calculate the probability of a male child with that genotype.
